title: Japan's Record Bond Auction Meets Brent at $109 as Yields Test Two-Decade Highs
subhead: Tokyo's 20-year JGB sale drew the strongest demand on record (bid-to-cover 5.84) even as 10-year Treasury yields touch their highest since 2002. Brent pushed back above $109 on Red Sea and Saudi infrastructure risk while the yen and yuan both firmed against the dollar.

sections.heading: Tokyo's record auction is not the good news it looks like
sections.body:
Japan's 20-year government bond auction on Tuesday drew a bid-to-cover ratio of 5.84, the strongest on record, according to Bloomberg and NDTV Profit. Domestic institutions were reported to have net-bought ¥18.8 trillion of JGBs in the first fiscal half. The immediate market effect was a firmer yen and a softer dollar, with the 10-year JGB yield near a three-decade peak.

The nuance matters: a record bid-to-cover at these levels is a story about price, not about confidence. Investors are showing up because long-end yields have finally repriced to something worth owning after years of yield-curve control. Reuters has reported the 10-year JGB yield hitting a three-decade high on inflation worries, and Nikkei Asia has described super-long JGB yields marching toward 3% on fiscal fears tied to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending promises.

Meanwhile a Reuters poll published Tuesday night found 69% of economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates to 1.50% in December, keeping to its quarterly tightening pace rather than moving at the October meeting. Brokerages surveyed by Reuters expect further tightening into 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is the world's largest foreign holder of US Treasuries and the funding source for a decade of carry trades. A record auction at three-decade yields means Japanese institutions now have a domestic alternative that pays. That is the quiet mechanism behind the simultaneous rise in US and European long-end yields.

sections.heading: The long end is repricing everywhere at once
sections.body:
Tuesday's session saw an unusually synchronized move: Reuters reported a global bond rout pushing US Treasury yields to a 24-year peak, with Forbes putting the 10-year at its highest level since 2002. That is not a single-country story — it is the long end of the global curve resetting simultaneously in Tokyo, Washington and Paris.

The US leg softened late in the session. Reuters reported that a strong 10-year note auction helped US bonds sell-off ease and yields come off their highs, and CNBC reported yields falling from multiyear highs by Wednesday morning Asian trade. But the level, not the daily direction, is the point: the US is borrowing at 2002 prices.

The dollar reflected that push-pull. Reuters reported the dollar dipping as traders weighed Iran and AI-related risks, with the euro edging up despite French unrest. Sterling had surged earlier on UK jobs data before consolidating.
sections.whyItMatters: Higher long-end yields across all three major blocs is the most consequential macro fact of the week. It raises the cost of refinancing sovereign debt precisely when France, Japan and the US are all running large deficits — and it tightens global financial conditions without any central bank moving.

sections.heading: France's spread holds above 150bp with a Moody's review on the doorstep
sections.body:
French 10-year yields dipped Tuesday but remained near a 24-year high in volatile trading, Reuters reported. The OAT-Bund spread topped 150 basis points and the euro held near $1.12 ahead of a Moody's review on Friday, according to FinanceFeeds. Bloomberg reported a French bond-risk gauge breaching a key level after the weekend protests.

Credit default swaps have moved toward 2013 highs, per Investing.com reporting carried by Yahoo Finance. The political backdrop is deteriorating rather than stabilising: the BBC reported France remains divided over blame for the weekend riots, a suspect was arrested after a historic town hall was set alight, and CNBC reported the government will deploy military forces ahead of fresh unrest this weekend.

Notably, contagion has been contained. The Wall Street Journal reported French contagion is less virulent than in previous eurozone crises, and UBS argued a French downgrade poses limited contagion risk to EU credit, according to IndexBox. Moody's itself said it sees no quick resolution of French political fragmentation, per Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is pricing French political risk, not French solvency — and the distinction is holding so far because Italy and Spain spreads have not blown out. Friday's Moody's decision is the next binary event. A downgrade without contagion would confirm the market is treating France as an isolated political risk; a downgrade with spread widening in Rome or Madrid would be a different story entirely.

sections.heading: Brent back above $109 as the Hormuz risk premium refuses to decay
sections.body:
Brent crude rose 85 cents, or 0.78%, to $109.64 a barrel in Wednesday Asian trade, with WTI up 76 cents to $98.58, Reuters reported. The prior session had seen Brent settle down 0.69% at $108.79 after touching a five-month high of $111.99.

The trigger is physical, not speculative. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said a supertanker caught fire after striking a sea mine south of the Strait of Hormuz while violating Iranian regulations, per Iranian media cited by Reuters. Shiptracker Kpler counted at least 18 vessel attacks over two weeks. LSEG analysts noted attacks have expanded beyond Hormuz as far south as the Gulf of Oman, threatening loadings outside the Arab Gulf and the ship-to-ship transfers holding Middle East exports together.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on a Saudi Aramco site at Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and Riyadh and Abha airports. The IMO's secretary-general, Arsenio Dominguez, told Fox News that the traffic separation scheme still has mines and that the organisation cannot guarantee a transiting vessel will not be hit.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran's proposal to reopen the strait within seven days remains on the table and that the waterway stays shut until Washington accepts its conditions, per Gulf News. Iran has received no response from Saudi Arabia or the Houthis to its offer to broker talks.
sections.whyItMatters: Oil at $109 with a live mine threat is a tax on every importer and a direct input to the Federal Reserve's inflation problem. Iran's seven-day offer is the only de-escalation path on the table, and it is being ignored. The freight market is already adjusting — Reuters reported Asian refiners switching to smaller tankers and buying delivered crude as freight rates soar.

sections.heading: The RBA's inflation problem is getting worse, not better
sections.body:
Reserve Bank of Australia deputy governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook has deteriorated materially — slightly above the RBA's own expectations — ahead of the November 3 board meeting, per ABC and Reuters. The Guardian framed it as shortening odds of a fifth rate hike this year; the Australian Financial Review reported hard choices await the RBA as both inflation and employment worsen.

The currency responded: the Australian dollar was buoyed by the hawkish tone in Wednesday trade, Reuters reported. The backdrop is a run of higher-than-expected inflation prints that has already forced Commonwealth Bank economists to shift their call to a November rate rise, per CommBank, and led Bloomberg to report speculative investors betting on a November hike back in August.
sections.whyItMatters: Australia is now the clearest case of a developed central bank being forced to tighten into a slowing economy because of an energy-driven inflation impulse it cannot control. If the RBA hikes on November 3, it will be the first G10 central bank this cycle to admit the disinflation trade is over.

sections.heading: The yuan hits a four-year high and Beijing lets it
sections.body:
The yuan reached a four-year high against the dollar and its basket after China's Q3 GDP growth accelerated to 4.5%, beating forecasts, per Reuters and CNBC. Bloomberg had reported earlier in October that the PBOC was backing its FX policy and allowing the currency to strengthen versus the basket.

The macro logic is straightforward: stronger growth reduces the urgency for new stimulus, and a firmer currency reduces imported inflation and capital-outflow pressure. Strong Chinese growth and a strong currency also help the trade story — though South Korean and Japanese export data show the region's outperformance is concentrated in semiconductors, with South Korea's October 1-20 exports up 105% on record chip sales and Japan's September exports up 16.7%, slower than forecast.
sections.whyItMatters: A stronger yuan without PBOC intervention is a small but real shift toward letting markets do more of the work on capital flows. It also raises the political value of the currency ahead of any Trump-Xi meeting — a stronger yuan addresses Washington's oldest complaint about Chinese trade practice at zero fiscal cost to Beijing.

sections.heading: A New Jersey cheese importer sues over the Canada tariffs
sections.body:
The Liberty Justice Center filed a lawsuit on behalf of Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey food importer, asking the US Court of International Trade to strike down the White House's 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods and order refunds with interest, the BBC reported. The firm is paying 50% duties on Canadian cheese while also facing Canadian retaliation on its US-made cheese exports.

The legal theory is narrow and interesting: the administration invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a near-century-old provision aimed at foreign discrimination. The plaintiffs argue it does not authorise sweeping tariffs, that it has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and that the required 30-day waiting period was breached — duties on cheese were added a week before collection began.

The White House imposed the levies after trade talks with Canada broke down in August, and Prime Minister Mark Carney matched them dollar-for-dollar last month.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the same legal vehicle that previously succeeded against the 'liberation day' tariffs. If Section 338 also falls, the administration loses its fastest unilateral tariff instrument — and the refund liability for importers already paying becomes a fiscal question, not just a trade one.

bottomLine: Today's through-line is that sovereign borrowing costs are being repriced simultaneously in Tokyo, Washington and Paris, and none of it is driven by central bank decisions. Japan's record 20-year auction drew the strongest demand ever only because yields finally pay; US 10-year yields sit at 2002 levels; France's spread holds above 150bp into a Friday Moody's review. Add Brent at $109 on live mine attacks in Hormuz and the RBA warning that inflation is worse than it thought, and you get a global financial system absorbing an energy shock while paying two-decade prices for government debt. The absence of contagion from France so far is the one piece of genuinely good news — and it depends on what Moody's says on Friday.
